Retrieval-Augmented Generation

CHAPTER 1
INTRODUCTION
Many students still struggle to grasp complex academic content, which can
lead to suboptimal learning outcomes across various educational contexts. In
higher education, the sheer quantity and complexity of lecture notes often
overwhelm students without immediate contextual assistance, making it difficult
for them to process and retain information effectively, which can hinder students'
understanding and academic performance (Binkley, 2023). Though lecture notes
are designed to provide students with detailed information, it can often hinder
rather than support effective learning. Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) explains that
learners have a limited working memory capacity, and when instructional
materials are too lengthy or poorly structured, they impose unnecessary intrinsic
and extraneous cognitive load. This overload prevents students from processing
information efficiently and transferring knowledge into long-term memory. In the
context of online learning, where students rely heavily on digital lecture materials,
extended notes without proper segmentation or instructional design may lead to
confusion, fatigue, and disengagement. Studies have shown that learning content
quality strongly influences both e-learning quality and student satisfaction,
highlighting the importance of managing cognitive load in instructional design. Thus, instead of aiding comprehension, extended lecture notes may
unintentionally reduce learning outcomes by overwhelming students and
diminishing their ability to retain essential concepts. (Abeysekera et al., 2024)
Artificial intelligence has emerged as a transformative force. With the rise of
large language models, the landscape of artificial intelligence has significantly
transformed, with its applications spreading across various domains as these models
are characterized by their ability to generate human-like text. This has
revolutionized tasks such as natural language understanding, translation,
summarization, and question answering (QA) that were previously constrained by
the limitations of traditional rule-based systems and smaller task-specific
models. Advances in LLMs have led to an increase in practical use, offering real-
time support to help students clarify their doubts and enhance their learning
experience (Roumeliotis & Tselikas, 2023).

However, while LLMs have significant
benefits, they present problems and limitations. A notable drawback is the risk of
the model hallucinating, where the AI generates responses that are incorrect,
nonsensical, or unfaithful to the provided source content (Ji et al., 2023). Additionally, because LLMs primarily relies on learned data, it may be challenging
to update or extend their knowledge base in real-time (Oche et al., 2025). A solution that can be utilized is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). A
hybrid approach that combines the generative power of LLMs with the ability to
retrieve real-time information from external sources, such as databases or the
1
THESIS TITLE HERE

internet. This hybrid approach grounds that the responses generated by the AI to be
accurate and up to date to the information retrieved, thus reducing the likelihood of
hallucinations and improving the overall reliability of the system (Lewis
et al., 2020). RAG holds promise in educational settings, where it is critical for
student to have accurate, contextually relevant information to support their learning
(Swacha & Gracel, 2025). However, while there are numerous studies on enhancing
LLMs through RAG, but research into its practical application in the education
sector, particularly in helping students understand and learn from their university
lecture notes, remains underexplored.

This opens an opportunity to explore the topic. We introduce Qubo, a
retrieval-augmented question answering system designed to support student
learning through accurate and contextually grounded responses. The system relies
on RAG to integrate a knowledge base wherein it seeks relevant information that
helps it retain factual consistency to ensure students still retain knowledge from the
sources. This study covers the design and development of Qubo, we aim to
investigate its effectiveness in providing accuracy and reliability in providing
learning support and assess whether this AI-driven system can be a reliable
alternative form of learning method for students. 2
THESIS TITLE HERE

1.1 BACKGROUND OF THE STUDY
Use of AI or artificial intelligence is becoming more and more prevalent in schools to
assist with such things as personal learning automated grading and even paper handling. Research indicates that AI has enormous potential for increasing student productivity and
accessibility but also poses fears over the effect it will have on education. Problems such
as as less human contact, privacy concerns, algorithm bias, and unequal access to
technology need to be confronted. To reap the most of AI without succumbing to its harms,
Al-Zahrani (2024) suggests a well-balanced strategy that couple's innovation with ethics,
teacher training, and openness. Students have increasingly started relying on AI-powered chatbots. Large
language models (LLMs), such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, provide instant explanations,
feedback, and answers to questions. Many students find this helpful because it aids them
in asking about topics, they have a hard time understanding. Research also shows that
these chatbots can boost engagement and confidence, especially in online courses where
teacher interaction is limited [8]. For example, in a study on an R programming course,
students reported that the chatbot helped them solve complex problems not covered in
lectures, and many even requested similar tools for other classes [4].During the first year
of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers analyzed how U.S. high school students reflected
on their educational experiences. A lot of students reported difficulties with time
management, friendships, and mental health. Most also said their academic performance,
motivation, social life, self-control, and job preparedness were negatively affected. Still,
students noted some benefits, such as becoming more self-reliant, improving their use of
digital technologies, and developing a greater appreciation for their professors. The study
further showed that while the class of 2023 and students from less advantaged families
faced greater struggles, effective educational support and opportunities for in-person
learning helped reduce these challenges [18]. Another study looked at how the mental health of freshmen affects their academic
performance. It found that students struggling with mental health issues often received
lower grades. On the other hand, those who adjusted well to college life and believed in
their own academic abilities were better able to overcome challenges. In short, good
mental health, adaptability, and confidence in learning work together to help students
succeed [17]. However, LLMs also come with challenges. One of the biggest problems is
what researchers call “hallucinations,” where the model generates answers that sound
convincing but are wrong or misleading. This creates serious issues when used in
sensitive areas such as education, healthcare, or privacy.

Ji et al. (2023) argue that better
evaluation methods and stronger safeguards are needed to make these systems more
reliable [2]. A promising solution to this problem is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Instead of relying only on what the model has learned during training, RAG combines
LLMs with external sources of accurate information, grounding responses in real data. Early studies show that RAG-based chatbots are more reliable but also effective for
education, since they provide course-specific and trustworthy support [4]. This makes
RAG an important step forward in using AI responsibly in education, offering students
better learning experiences while addressing the weaknesses of traditional LLMs, such as
hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and transparent reasoning when implemented
properly. By connecting LLMs to outside information sources, Retrieval-Augmented
3
THESIS TITLE HERE

Generation (RAG) can address these problems and potentially improve accuracy and
validity.[19]. This study explores how AI technologies help in modern learning challenges
through the utilization of RAG in the development of Qubo, a chatbot specialized for
source-grounded student learning. This study will be valuable not only to students seeking
alternative, reliable learning support but also to educators exploring supplementary
approaches to facilitate student learning. The insights derived from this study can be used
to widen the knowledge on how to effectively use AI for reliable learning. Moreover, the
research can help shape the future development of AI-assisted learning tools, offering
educators a deeper understanding of how these systems can be used to foster
independent learning and improve engagement among students. The study strives to
facilitate a much better understanding of how supplementary AI tools can be integrated
into the education sector to help enhance student learning. This study is especially
relevant in the context of the Philippines, where education is highly valued, yet access to
quality educational resources remains a challenge in many regions By examining the
potential of Qubo and similar AI tools, this study aims to highlight how AI-powered learning
platforms can serve as an accessible and scalable solution to enhance student
engagement and academic performance, particularly in regions where traditional learning
methods may fall short. 1.2 STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM
The increasing complexity and volume of information in modern education
present significant challenges for students trying to effectively learn and retain key
concepts from lectures. While lecture notes are a key resource, they are often dense,
incomplete, or lack explanations that are easy to understand, limiting students ability to
graph complex topics and slowing down their learning. Specifically, the problems are as
follows:
1. Difficulty in Understanding Lecture Notes
Students frequently struggle to learn from lecture notes alone because the
content can be fragmented and lacks sufficient context, making it difficult to connect
concepts and fully grasp complex topics. 2. Limited Access to Immediate Clarification
The traditional learning process is often reliant on students' manual review of
notes and does not provide immediate support from the Instructor. This leaves students
with unanswered questions that can hinder their overall understanding.

3. Overload and Fragmentation of Learning Resources
4
THESIS TITLE HERE

The sheer volume and scattered nature of academic content can overwhelm
students, leading to a weak understanding of core ideas and continuing knowledge
gaps. 4. Inefficient and slow learning
The challenge in navigating dense and incomplete notes slows down the learning
process, making it difficult for students to absorb information and retain key concepts.

5. Overwhelming Teacher Workload
Teachers' overwhelming workloads, due to large class sizes and numerous
administrative responsibilities, often prevent them from giving individualized attention to
each student
1.3 OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY
General Objective
The general objective of this study is to develop a chatbot platform using Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) to help students learn from academic lecture notes, while
ensuring accuracy and credibility through content sourced directly from academic
materials. Specific Objectives
Develop a chatbot that supports student learning by integrating Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) with a large language model (LLM) to provide accurate
and contextually relevant answers sourced from trusted academic materials. Develop an upload module that allows students to submit their lecture notes or
study materials to the platform, enabling the chatbot to use the contents for accurate and
personalized retrieval during interactions. Enhance the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline to improve the
accuracy and efficiency of capturing and retrieving relevant student notes. 1.4 SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY
5
THESIS TITLE HERE

Theoretical Significance
The study contributes to the progression of AI integration in the education sector. By utilizing RAG with Large Language Models(LLMs) to provide reliable and contextually
relevant answers, the study showcases how AI has the potential to revolutionize how
learning resources are accessed and utilized. The findings from this research can help
overcome the limitation of traditional Large Language Models(LLMs), particularly the issue
of “hallucination,” and demonstrate a more robust framework for using AU to support
learning. Lastly, this approach may pave the path for future advances in instructional
technology and tailored learning.

Practical Significance
The study directly addresses a critical challenge in modern education: the gap
between the information in lecture notes and a student's ability to effectively understand
and retain it. By developing a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot, this
research provides a practical and innovative solution that benefits key stakeholders and
advances the field of educational technology. The study will provide students with a tool for independent learning. By offering
immediate, accurate, and context-specific answers drawn directly from their own lecture
notes, the RAG chatbot will help students overcome common learning hurdles, such as
fragmented information and difficulty in understanding complex concepts, learning to
improve information retention and academic performance. For instructors and academic institutions, this study provides a solution that
improves efficiency and educational quality. The chatbot eases the strain on teachers by
automating responses to common student questions, freeing up crucial time. This enables
educators to focus on more important practical duties, such as creating compelling classes
and providing in-depth support for challenging topics. The effective application of this
technology can serve as an example for schools seeking to integrate AI-powered tools
into a more efficient and modern learning environment. 6
THESIS TITLE HERE

1.5 SCOPE AND LIMITATION
Scope
The purpose of this study is to create a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
chatbot that will help students in asking enquires using academic lecture notes. The
system's primary function is to allow students to upload digital lecture notes like PDF which
are eventually processed into a knowledge base for retrieval and response generation. The chatbot uses a large language model (LLM) and a retrieval pipeline to generate
responses that are grounded in the uploaded documents. It covers the design, development, and testing of the chatbot as a prototype
learning tool. It highlights basics such as document intake, knowledge retrieval, and
natural language answer development, making it helpful in both the classroom and self-
study settings.

The system's target audience are students at a certain school who regularly
use lecture notes as their primary learning resource. The system developed in this study can handle file types such as pdf, docx, and
text files. The system support multiple uploads simotaneously and
Functional testing and user-based assessment are the only methods used to
evaluate the system. These methods focus on the chatbot's accuracy, efficiency in
collecting information from lecture notes, and efficiency in assisting independent study. This limitation offers a proof-of-concept that illustrates the possibilities of RAG-powered
chatbots in education, but it excludes extensive implementation and integration with
learning management systems (LMS). Furthermore, even though the study's primary
focus is on text-based lecture notes, other file formats—like pictures, handwritten notes,
and multimedia—are not included and are instead being explored as potential areas for
improvement. Limitations
7
THESIS TITLE HERE

This study adheres to current privacy and ethical regulations, ensuring that all
practices align with industry standards. A key limitation in this research is the use of
academic notes and proprietary materials, which may raise concerns regarding intellectual
property and privacy. Given the sensitivity of using such materials, the study deliberately
avoids relying on academic notes or restrictions. Instead, it uses open-access lectures
and publicly available educational content for demonstration purposes. The Chabot developed in the study can only support PDF's, word, and text files. It cannot process files such as HTML, JSON, or domain specific file types. This limitation
is due to the differences in the preprocessing logic of every file type. Additionally, the
system currently lacks the capability to capture images if there exist in the documents,
due to the system lacks of integration of multimodal tools such as Optical Image
Recognition and Multimodal Large Language Models because of resource and budget
constraints, though the logic in implementation of the system in this study can be easily
adapted to support image recognition, which will be explained further in recommendations
for future work. This study was conducted within the constraints of available resources, including
time, budget, and computational capacity. As a result, the implementation focuses on a
feasible and manageable approach suitable for a prototype or proof-of-concept. While this
allows for the demonstration of the core concepts, it may limit scalability, performance, or
the inclusion of more advanced features.

These aspects are acknowledged as potential
directions for future work. Another limitation of the platform developed in this study is that while it allows users
to upload dynamic data, it is not fully equipped to control or monitor the types of content
that users may upload. Although the platform is designed primarily as a chatbot for
accessing lecture notes and educational resources, there is a risk that users might upload
data or generate prompts that fall outside the intended scope of the system. The platform’s
open-ended nature means that users might misuse the system for generating unintended
or inappropriate prompts, which could lead to responses that are not aligned with the
educational objectives. For example, some users may upload irrelevant or non-
educational materials or even attempt to prompt the system to produce content unrelated
to the learning environment. 8
THESIS TITLE HERE

CHAPTER 2
REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES
2.1 RELATED LITERATURES
Challenges in Education
It was tackles complete literature review discussed on the difficulties in the
implementation of the Special Education (SPED) curriculum in the Philippines. Even in
the face of current legislation and policies to facilitate access to learning, schools
continue to face obstacles in such areas as inadequate resources, insufficient teacher
preparation, and policy practice discrepancy. Racism towards dis- brought about by
disability, and finan- abled students and family financial cial barriers are the main
obstacles to constraints are barriers to effective special education implementation. These are challenges that result in gaps in the provision of quality education, particularly
in rural areas.

According to the report, developing SPED services requires an increased
government budget, effective teacher training, policy consistency, public awareness, and
family support[13]. Cognitive load from extensive learning notes
The study about The Effect of Cognitive Load on Learning Memory in the accounting
student in the Philippines emphasizes that intrinsic and extrinsic cognitive load must be
reduced to enhance students’ learning efficiency. This aligns with the idea that extended
lecture materials, when not carefully designed, may overwhelm students’ working
memory. Thus, cognitive difficulties arise when learners struggle to process and store
excessive or poorly structured lecture content. The findings highlight that improving LMS quality and reducing extraneous load can
directly support students’ comprehension. This connects with challenges in
understanding extended lecture notes, where clarity, pacing, and organization are
essential for preventing overload. When lecture materials are fragmented or overly
complex, students’ working memory becomes strained, reducing comprehension. The results also showed that satisfaction and improved e-learning quality enhance long-
term memory retention. This indicates that properly managed instructional design can
mitigate comprehension problems in lecture materials. In contrast, extended lecture
notes without supportive structure or digital scaffolds may weaken both memory storage
and motivation, further illustrating the difficulty students face in understanding them. (sunga et al 2024) (local)
https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/16/4/1686
Learners interacting with digital lecture materials often encounter increased cognitive
demands. Extended digital content requires sustained attention and the simultaneous
processing of multiple elements, which can overwhelm working memory and reduce
9
THESIS TITLE HERE

comprehension efficiency. The cognitive load imposed by digital formats highlights the
importance of designing learning materials that account for students’ limited mental
resources. Digital environments can slow learners’ processing and response times, particularly for
complex or detailed information. When cognitive resources are stretched, students may
rely on surface-level processing strategies, such as memorization, rather than engaging
in deeper cognitive strategies like organizing, elaborating, or monitoring information. This
can hinder the ability to fully understand and retain extended lecture materials delivered
digitally. These findings imply that digital lecture content must be carefully structured to minimize
extraneous cognitive load and support meaningful learning. Incorporating strategies that
promote attention management, reduce perceptual and structural disruptions, and
encourage active engagement can help learners process and retain digital materials
more effectively.

Without such support, extended digital content may lead to persistent
difficulties in comprehension and memory retention. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10639-025-13668-5?utm (international)
The Role of AI and Machine Learning in Education
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is positively transforming higher education, reshaping
how students learn and how teachers teach academics (Zouhaier, 2023). Instead of
traditional methods, educational institutions are adopting these technologies to keep up
with the innovation of our rapidly changing world (Tsou, 2023; Arthur D. Little, 2024). Important AI subfields like machine learning (ML) and natural language processing,
which enable AI systems to evaluate student data and modify lessons to suit different
learning styles and speeds, are at the center of this integration. Better learning outcomes are achieved through individualized instruction,
specialized tutoring programs, and quicker evaluation of student work thanks to this
personalized approach. AI helps teachers at the same time by automating tedious
chores and guaranteeing that students receive insightful and consistent feedback (Harry,
2023). It discovers highlights on how artificial intelligence (AI) is improving education
through providing personalized learning, developing grading systems, and helping
teachers in providing more effective training. Its emphasizes the benefits of AI, such as
adaptive learning tools, automation grading, and insights based on data that improve
teaching and learning. At the same time, it recognizes challenges such as ethical
factors, data protection, usability problems and the need for educators to have enough
training. Overall, the study focuses on AI's potential to improve education while
emphasizing the significance of accessibility, transparency, and ethical
responsibility[12]. 10
THESIS TITLE HERE

Student learning through AI
In the Philippine educational context, the integration of AI offers a multitude of
opportunities for enhancing the overall learning experience. AI-driven tools are
increasingly seen as a way to augment educators, helping them better understand
students' learning progress and tailor teaching strategies accordingly (Estrellado &
Miranda, 2023). While the prospects of AI integration in the Philippine industry are
promising, the progress is still in its early stages. Important issues such as privacy
concerns, data security, and the potential for widening the digital divide are critical
challenges that must be explicitly addressed (Holmes et al., 2021, as cited in Estrellado
& Miranda, 2023). While AI's impact on education is broad, its most significant contribution lies in
directly supporting student learning by making it more personalized, engaging, and
efficient. AI technologies like machine learning and natural language processing analyze
student data to tailor the educational experience to each individual’s pace and learning
style (Harry, 2023). This leads to improved outcomes through personalized learning
systems, intelligent tutoring, and automated grading, which save teachers time and
provide consistent feedback
Chatbots powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) in Student Learning
Chatbots that are powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) has changed the
way students interact with learning materials by providing personalized on-demand
support. These advanced AI technologies, such as OpenAI's GPT models, can improve
student learning by responding instantly to questions, providing thorough explanations,
and adjusting to different learning styles. This individualized learning experience is
especially effective in increasing engagement since students can get quick help with
homework, clarify concepts, or explore topics further without having to wait for a
teacher's availability (Ayala & Béchard, 2024).

The ability to receive immediate feedback
and support enhances learning and keeps students engaged, especially in self-paced
situations where they can study at their own pace. Some of the main features of LLM-powered chatbots is their capacity to give
specific learning experiences. These chatbots assess students' questions and adjust
responses to their level of knowledge, ensuring that explanations are clear and relevant. It proves particularly helpful for several classrooms with students of different degree of
competency in different topics (Gupta et al., 2024). Chatbots can assist students narrow
learning gaps and provide additional support by providing guidance that is customized to
their requirements. Furthermore, the ability of these chatbots to handle repeated
questions or commonly requested topics frees up significant time for instructors to focus
on advanced parts of education, therefore enhancing the entire learning experience. However, with their potential, LLM-powered chatbots are limited. They can also
generate wrong or incomplete responses, a condition known as hallucination, in which
the chatbot offers answers that seem logical but are inaccurate in fact (Lewis et al.,
2020). This can be particularly challenging in educational environments when accuracy
is critical to student learning. Furthermore, while chatbots thrive at presenting factual
information, they may struggle with higher-order cognitive tasks like encouraging critical
11
THESIS TITLE HERE

analysis or facilitating deeper conversations. As a result, while they can be an effective
additional tool, they should be used along with traditional teaching approaches to ensure
that students receive full and reliable information. Despite these challenges, chatbots in education provide substantial benefits,
particularly in terms of active learning. Students can interact with chatbots by asking
follow-up questions and receiving personalized explanations, which improves retention
and understanding. In addition, the usage of chatbots promotes self-directed learning by
allowing students to revisit topics, test their knowledge, and receive quick feedback, this
supporting continual learning and development. Chatbots act as both tutors and learning
companions, assisting students in achieving their academic goals more successfully. Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a solution to mitigate
some of the challenges faced by LLMs, particularly hallucination and limited knowledge
generalization (Lewis et al, 2020; Ayala & Béchard, 2024; Kirchenbauer & Barns, 2024). RAG is an architecture designed to enhance LLMs by first searching for useful information
before responding, rather than answering solely based on the LLM's learned knowledge
from training. Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on vast volumes of data and
use billions of parameters to generate original output for tasks like answering questions,
translating languages, and completing sentences. RAG can extend the already powerful
capabilities of LLMs by grounding its responses in specific domains or an organization's
internal knowledge base without retraining the model(Gupta et al., 2024). RAG models
can ground outputs in reliable documents, ensuring responses are both relevant and
verifiable, which could be beneficial for dealing with educational materials. Fig. 1 shows the basic process of how LLMs work. When a user submits a query,
the model processes the input and generates a response. The input can be any text, like
a question or statement. The LLM (such as GPT or LLaMA) starts by breaking the input
into smaller parts called tokens, which represent words or subwords.nNext, the model
uses a mechanism called self-attention to understand how these tokens relate to each
other. This helps the model understand the meaning of the query.

After processing the
input, the model predicts the next word or phrase based on what it has learned. It
generates the response step-by-step, using the previous words to predict what comes
12
THESIS TITLE HERE

next. Finally, the model displays the generated text as its response, ensuring it is relevant
and coherent based on the input. Figure 2 illustrates how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the
functionality of LLMs. The approach can be broken down into three main stages:
Indexing: In this stage documents into chunks and uses an ending model to turn those
chunk into a vector along with its text representation and metadata. Each of these are then
stored into a vector database to where the retriever searcher for relevant information. Retrieval: Before generating a response, RAG searches an external knowledge base (e.g.,
PDFs, DOCX files, or web content). The input query and relevant documents are
vectorized, meaning they are converted into numerical representations that capture the
semantic meaning of the content. Typically, vectorization techniques like BERT
embeddings or Sentence-BERT are used for creating these vectors. The vectorized
documents are then stored in a vector database for efficient similarity-based retrieval. The
most relevant documents are retrieved
Generation: The most relevant documents retrieved during the retrieval phase are used
to provide context for the LLM. These documents, combined with the model's learned
knowledge, inform the generation of a response. This ensures that the model’s output is
not only based on the data it was trained on but also grounded in specific, relevant
13
THESIS TITLE HERE

information retrieved from external sources, thereby enhancing the accuracy and
relevance of the response. However, aspects like tone, fluency, and coherence are still
primarily handled by the LLM’s pre-existing knowledge, as the model generates the
response based on both the retrieved context and its trained language capabilities.

React and Fast API as an app development stack
React is a declarative, component-based library that allows developers to build
reusable UI components. Its modular architecture enables the creation of highly
interactive and responsive user interfaces that update dynamically as data changes,
while preserving a clear separation of concerns. These characteristics make React
particularly well-suited for applications where an engaging user experience is a priority
(React, n.d.). On the server side, FastAPI is a modern, high-performance Python web
framework built on Starlette and Pydantic. It is designed to maximize both speed and
developer productivity by providing features such as automatic data validation, type
annotations, and interactive API documentation through OpenAPI and Swagger. Its
asynchronous architecture enables the handling of many concurrent requests, making it
particularly suitable for real-time applications and microservices. Moreover, using
FastAPI as a backend solution facilitates seamless integration with the extensive
ecosystem of Python machine learning libraries, allowing developers to incorporate
advanced data processing and AI capabilities directly into their applications (FastAPI,
n.d.). 14

When combined, React and FastAPI provide a robust stack for modern app
development: React manages the frontend presentation and interactivity, while FastAPI
powers the backend logic, APIs, and data processing. This separation of concerns
promotes scalability, maintainability, and rapid development, making the stack
particularly effective for building data-driven applications such as AI-powered chatbot
applications. 2.2 RELATED STUDIES
Enhancing student learning through Generative AI
Recent research in Metro Manila shows how students are beginning to engage with
generative AI technologies in their academic work. Arguson, Paculanan, and Mabborang
(2024) found that while students are generally open to using AI for homework, their
acceptance largely depends on their attitudes toward the tools, their confidence in using
them, and the accessibility of these systems. Among AI platforms, ChatGPT was the most
familiar and widely used compared to Copilot and Gemini. These findings suggest that the
Philippine education system is not only facing legal and ethical challenges but is also
experiencing a cultural shift as students increasingly view AI as a learning partner
(Arguson, Paculanan, & Mabborang, 2024). A separate study looked at how instructors in community colleges in Albay, Philippines,
are incorporating AI into student performance assessments. The research highlights
several benefits, including opportunities for personalized learning and improved
evaluation, but it also points out challenges such as limited facilities, lack of training, and
ethical concerns about privacy and fairness.

Results indicate that while both students and
educators recognize AI’s potential, there are still significant gaps in confidence, equal
access, and ethical awareness—especially among part-time instructors. To address these
issues, the study proposes an AI framework focused on monitoring, operational security,
and instructional support to ensure ethical and effective AI integration in education
(Tabuena, 2025). Similarly, the article Generative AI and Education: Dynamic Personalization of Pupils’
School Learning Material with ChatGPT explores how ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 can be used in
primary education to personalize lessons. In a study of 110 Uruguayan pupils aged 8–14,
15
THESIS TITLE HERE

generative AI was used to adapt history lessons—texts, illustrations, and exercises—
based on students’ knowledge levels. The results showed that AI-driven personalization
improved motivation, engagement, and performance by supporting intrinsic motivation
and creating a sense of “flow” in learning. Still, the study cautions against overreliance on
AI and raises concerns about data privacy and accessibility. Overall, the findings suggest
that, when used thoughtfully, generative AI can significantly enhance pupils’ learning
experiences (Jauhiainen & Garagorry Guerra, 2024). Meanwhile, the article Enhancing Student Engagement Through Artificial Intelligence (AI):
Understanding the Basics, Opportunities, and Challenges introduces the core concepts of
AI and examines its role in reshaping higher education. It explains how tools such as
generative AI and chatbots can personalize instruction, provide adaptive feedback, and
encourage interactive learning across different contexts. The authors also emphasize
critical concerns, including ethical issues, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and risks to
academic integrity. The paper concludes by calling for more research on adaptive
systems, ethical AI practices, and collaborative learning models to maximize the benefits
of AI while ensuring fairness and student well-being (Nguyen, Kremantzis, Essien,
Petrounias, & Hosseini, 2024). Hallucination in LLMs
Recent Large Language Models(LLMs) have exponentially improved in fluency
due to the development of new solutions such as transformer-based architectures.

Challenges and Limitations of RAG
Despite the numerous virtues of incorporating RAG, several challenges need
attention. The retrieval mechanism, which is helpful for grounding answers in relevant
information, can still struggle, particularly when dealing with ambiguous queries or niche
knowledge domains. The Dense retrieval reliance on dense vector representation can
sometimes lead to irrelevant or off-topic documents being retrieved. Efforts to refine
retrieval techniques, including the incorporation of more sophisticated query expansion
and contextual disambiguation, are needed to improve performance in these areas. While
the integration of both retrieval and generation is seamless in theory, in practice, it may
break. The generative module may not effectively incorporate the relevant information in
its response. Research in enhancing the generation to have a better alignment
mechanism, such as improved attention models or hierarchical fusion techniques, may
help alleviate these issues. In the generation mechanism, it may face issues in flawed and inadequate data,
which can confuse the model into producing responses that are misleading, incomplete,
or contextually off-target. This limitation highlights the importance of ensuring the quality
and relevance of the retrieved information and the effectiveness of the augmentation
process by cleaning, filtering, and verifying to ensure the integrity and reliability of the
retrieved information. LLM models also have a token allowance. Meaning there is a limit
on the number of tokens it can process, tokens may vary in the input and output of the
model, and a proper RAG should respect this boundary to ensure the generation is
complete. There is also a challenge in structuring the retrieved information that is to be
presented to LLM.

LLM may miss out on extracting the most relevant information from
long structures of information. To address this issue, advanced RAG systems can employ
techniques such as diversity-aware ranking or information salience detection. By
prioritizing and ordering the retrieved examples based on their relevance, diversity, and
informative value, RAG systems can ensure a more balanced and effective presentation
of the information to the LLM. RAG systems can introduce additional latency as rag involves several steps. This

Introduction
Theoretical Framework
This study is anchored on theories and models in the fields of Information Retrieval and
Representation Learning, which together provide the foundation for the Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm. First, Information Retrieval (IR) Theory explains the process of locating relevant
information from large document collections. Classical IR models, such as the Vector
Space Model (Salton, 1975) and the Probabilistic Model (Robertson & Sparck Jones,
1976), established how documents and queries can be represented mathematically, and
how similarity measures (e.g., cosine similarity, BM25) can rank documents based on
relevance. These theories support the role of the retriever component in RAG, where the
system identifies the most relevant passages to a user query.

Second, the study draws from Representation Learning Theory in Natural Language
Processing (NLP), which underpins modern dense retrieval methods. Word embeddings
(Mikolov et al., 2013), contextual embeddings (Devlin et al., 2019 with BERT), and
sentence transformers demonstrate how language can be mapped into high-dimensional
vector spaces where semantic similarity can be captured beyond mere keyword matching. This theoretical foundation justifies the use of dense encoders in RAG systems for
retrieving semantically relevant documents. Finally, Generative Language Model Theory (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020)
explains how large-scale transformer models can generate coherent and contextually
appropriate responses. When combined with retrieval mechanisms, these models
overcome the limitations of closed-book generation by grounding responses in external
knowledge. Thus, RAG embodies a theoretical synthesis of retrieval-based systems
(which ensure factual grounding) and generation-based systems (which ensure fluency
and flexibility). 28

Semantic Chunking
Extracted documents usually is too long, which might cause the retriever to fetch
whole corpora which is unnecessary and intensive, to handle this, a chunking strategy is
applied. Chunking is the process of dividing long documents into smaller segments,
commonly referred to as chunks. Each chunk typically contains only a few hundred words,
allowing the retrieval system to search more precisely and return only the most relevant
segments in response to a query. A chunking strategy is crucial to keep relevant sections
together and ensure it doesn’t cut mid sentences. Traditional chunking approaches use
fixed counts of either word, sentence, or paragraph to determine the length of chunks. While this ensures that the text is manageable for retrieval and processing, it often
produces arbitrary cuts that fail to align with the semantic flow of the document. For
example, a definition may be split across two chunks, or an example may be separated
from the concept it explains. Such breaks reduce retrieval accuracy and increase the
likelihood of fragmented or incomplete responses. A strategy that is gaining popularity is semantic chunking wherein instead of
cutting in fixed lengths divides text into coherent units of meaning, ensuring that each
chunk contains a logically consistent idea. Instead of relying on static boundaries,
semantic chunking leverages embeddings which are mathematical representations of
sentences or paragraphs to measure semantic similarity. The process begins by splitting
a document into sentences. Each sentence is then transformed into an embedding vector
using a pre-trained sentence transformer MiniLM v6 a lightweight yet powerful
transformer-based model that achieves performance comparable to larger models (such
as BERT or RoBERTa) while requiring significantly fewer computational resources. The
36
THESIS TITLE HERE

v6 variant is a fine-tuned version of MiniLM, optimized specifically for semantic textual
similarity, clustering, and retrieval tasks. Consecutive embeddings are compared using similarity scores. When the
similarity between sentences drops below a threshold, it is treated as a natural boundary,
and a new chunk is created. This ensures that only semantically related sentences are
grouped together. Additionally, a sliding window with overlap is applied so that a few
sentences from the end of one chunk are repeated at the beginning of the next. This
prevents loss of context at boundaries and improves the model’s ability to maintain
continuity. A maximum token length constraint (e.g., 300–800 tokens) is also enforced to
keep chunks within the processing limits of large language models. Embedding
After documents are divided into chunks, each chunk must be converted into a
format that allows the retrieval system to efficiently compare their meanings. This is
accomplished through embeddings. An embedding is a numerical representation of text
in a high-dimensional space, where the distance between two vectors reflects their

Sparse Retrieval is a traditional method in information retrieval where both
documents and queries are represented as sparse vectors, meaning most of the entries
are zero since only the words that occur in the text receive non-zero values. Sparse
Retrieval works by matching exact terms between the query and documents, which is
made efficient through an inverted index. An inverted index is a data structure that maps
each word in the vocabulary to the list of documents that contain it, allowing the system
to quickly find all candidate documents for a query without scanning the entire collection. Once the relevant documents are retrieved, they are scored to determine how well they
match the query. An issue with keyword matching is that simply counting word
occurrences is not sufficient, since some words appear very frequently (like “the” or “is”)
and are less informative, while rarer words provide stronger signals of relevance. To handle this, the ranking function BM25 is used. BM25 is a Bag-of-Words
model, where the presence or frequency of terms is used for matching this improves
retrieval by balancing three key factors: the frequency of query terms within a document
(term frequency), how rare or informative those terms are across the entire collection
(inverse document frequency), and document length normalization so that longer
documents do not automatically receive higher scores. In this way, sparse retrieval
offers an efficient and interpretable approach to search, relying on keyword overlap
enhanced with statistical weighting. We utilized BM25 Ranking for our Sparse Retrieval

Hybrid Retrieval is an approach that combines both sparse retrieval methods and
dense retrieval methods, to take advantage of their complementary strengths. Sparse
retrieval excels at finding documents with exact keyword matches, while dense retrieval
captures semantic meaning even when different words are used. In hybrid retrieval, we
used score fusion, where the relevance scores from both sparse and dense systems are
combined to produce a final ranking. For example, a document may receive a BM25
score based on keyword overlap and a cosine similarity score based on embedding
similarity, and these scores are merged (through weighted addition, normalization, or
other fusion techniques). Empirical studies demonstrate that hybrid retrieval consistently
outperforms either method alone across a range of benchmarks [46, 47].

Large Language Model
In this project, we used a pretrained large language model (LLM) called Mistral-Instruct
to generate answers. Mistral is an open-source model family designed to be efficient and
high-performing while remaining lighter than larger models such as GPT-3 or LLaMA-2. The “Instruct” variant has been fine-tuned on instruction-following datasets, which means
it is better at understanding natural user prompts and producing context-aware, helpful
responses rather than free-form text. By using Mistral-Instruct, we leverage a model that
already carries strong general knowledge and language generation abilities without the
need for training from scratch. prompt Assembly
Prompt Assembly refers to the process of carefully constructing the input that is sent to
the large language model before it generates a response. Since LLMs are highly
sensitive to how instructions and context are phrased, assembling the prompt ensures
that the model has the right information in the right format to produce accurate and
useful answers. In our setup, prompt assembly typically involves combining several
components: the user’s query, the retrieved documents (and possibly reranked
passages), and a set of instructions or guidelines that tell the model how to use the
information. For example, the assembled prompt might first present the user’s question,
then include the most relevant pieces of text from the knowledge base, and finally add
explicit instructions such as “Answer concisely based only on the provided context.” By
structuring the prompt in this way, we reduce irrelevant or hallucinated responses and
guide the LLM toward generating clear, grounded, and instruction-aligned outputs. 2.2.1 Windowing
